outputs.L1:
The Normal Monster sings in the Green Sahara. The voice and offal of the image of God make Celtic noises in these lyrical hells. Hurricanes of reasoned musics reap the uncensored earth. The loquent consciousness of living things pours forth in torrential languages.

The elderly colloquists—the Spirit and the Flesh—are out of tongue. The Spirit is impaled upon the phallus. Phoenixes of Irish fires lighten the Occident with Ireland’s wings, flap pandemoniums of Olympian prose, and satinize the imperial Rose with Gaelic perfumes—England, the sadistic mother, embraces Erin.

Master of meteoric idiom, present: the Word made flesh and feeding upon itself with erudite fangs; the sanguine introspection of the womb; Don Juan of Judea upon a pilgrimage to the Libido; the press purring its lullabies to sanity; Christ capitalized, scourging incontrite usurers of destiny in hole-and-corner temples, and hanging the soul’s advertisements outside the ecclesiast’s Zoo.

A gravid day spawns guttural gargoyles upon the Tower of Babel—an Empyrean emporium where the rejector-recreator Joyce flashes the giant reflector on the sub rosa.
outputs.L2:
Across the verdant Sahara, the ordinary Beast raises its song.  
God’s likeness speaks through voice and entrails, sounding Celtic notes amid these poetic infernos.  
Tempests of deliberate music harvest the earth without censorship.  
The articulate awareness of all living creatures floods forth in languages.  
Those ancient conversationalists, Spirit and Flesh, have lost their speech.  
Spirit hangs pierced on the phallus.  
A phoenix born of Irish flame brightens the West with Ireland’s wings,  
stirs chaos through Olympian prose,  
and gives the imperial Rose the sheen of Gaelic fragrance.  
England, the cruel mother, clasps Erin to herself.  
Behold the master of the meteoric phrase:  
the Word embodied, devouring itself with learned teeth;  
the womb’s blood-red self-examination;  
Judea’s Don Juan journeying toward the Libido.  
The press hums soothing songs to reason.  
Christ, rendered in capitals, lashes unrepentant moneylenders of fate  
inside secretive, obscure sanctuaries,  
while the soul’s notices are hung outside the churchman’s menagerie.  
A pregnant day gives birth to throaty gargoyles on the Tower of Babel—  
a celestial marketplace where Joyce, rejecting and remaking,  
turns an immense searchlight upon what lies concealed.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents language and consciousness as chaotic, torrential forces capable of transforming both the natural landscape and the spiritual realm. Words do not merely describe reality; they flood, fracture, and recreate it. Thought itself seems unstable and overwhelming, moving with an energy that dissolves familiar boundaries between mind, body, nature, and the divine.

At the center of the poem is a conflict between spirit and flesh. This struggle is expressed through imagery that is at once violent, erotic, and religious, suggesting that bodily desire and spiritual aspiration cannot be neatly separated. Sacred symbols become entangled with sexuality and suffering, while acts of creation resemble both violation and revelation. The resulting tension challenges conventional distinctions between purity and corruption, salvation and sin.

Ireland emerges within this turbulent vision as a source of linguistic, imaginative, and cultural power. Its language and identity resist the oppressive embrace of imperial England, whose influence threatens to absorb or silence them. Yet Ireland is not portrayed simply as passive or defeated. Its cultural energy survives through verbal invention, historical memory, and artistic rebellion, turning language into a means of resistance against political and cultural domination.

The poem is equally critical of religious institutions and the press. Both are represented as commercialized and punitive forces that claim authority over sanity, morality, and the soul. Rather than offering truth or spiritual guidance, they categorize, discipline, and exploit individuals. Their power depends on manipulating public judgment and converting private suffering into doctrine, scandal, or profit.

Against these oppressive structures, James Joyce is celebrated as a radical “rejector-recreator.” He rejects inherited conventions, official histories, and established forms of language, but his rejection is also a creative act. Through inventive, erudite, and disruptive prose, Joyce exposes realities that conventional discourse conceals. His writing becomes an instrument of illumination: it reveals the hidden operations of desire, power, faith, nationality, and consciousness while remaking the language through which those realities can be understood.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents James Joyce as a figure of radical linguistic and cultural rebellion. Rather than treating language as a stable instrument, it transforms words into a volatile material that can be broken apart, fused, distorted, and remade. Puns, invented expressions, abrupt shifts in register, and densely layered allusions create a torrent of experimental wordplay that recalls Joyce’s own literary methods. Meaning is rarely singular or fixed; each phrase seems capable of opening into several histories, voices, and associations at once.

Within this verbal turbulence, surreal and mythic images mingle with religious, sexual, and political ones. Sacred language is brought into uneasy contact with the body, while legendary figures and rituals appear beside fragments of ordinary life. These collisions expose the tensions buried beneath respectable cultural forms. Religion can become both a source of spiritual intensity and an institution compromised by repression, hypocrisy, or fear. Sexual imagery similarly resists conventional divisions between purity and corruption, suggesting that the body remains inseparable from imagination, guilt, desire, and artistic creation.

The poem’s Anglo-Irish imagery places these conflicts within the history of colonialism and divided national identity. English is both the language imposed by empire and the medium Joyce bends to his own purposes. Irish memory, Catholic tradition, British authority, and European culture overlap without settling into harmony. Joyce’s rebellion is therefore not merely stylistic: his manipulation of language becomes a challenge to the institutions and inherited categories that attempt to define nationality, morality, belief, and acceptable art.

Joyce emerges as a “rejector-recreator,” an artist who refuses established forms but does not stop at destruction. He rejects the authority of church, empire, social convention, and standardized language, then uses their fragments to construct something new. The poem suggests that corrupted systems cannot simply be escaped, because they have already entered consciousness and shaped the words through which experience is understood. They must instead be exposed, dismantled, and imaginatively reassembled.

In this sense, the poem portrays artistic creation as both rebellion and revelation. Its difficult, excessive language illuminates hidden struggles within the self: conflicts between faith and doubt, submission and resistance, shame and desire, colonial inheritance and cultural independence. By remaking language, Joyce also remakes the possibilities of identity. The poem ultimately celebrates him as an artist who turns fracture into form, using verbal disorder to reveal the tangled forces that govern consciousness and to create a new freedom from the ruins of inherited authority.
outputs.L5:
## The Normal Monster

Everyone in the village feared the monster in the forest.

They said it had enormous claws, terrible teeth, and eyes that glowed beneath the moon. No one had ever seen it clearly, but that only made the stories grow.

One evening, a curious child named Mara entered the woods. Deep among the trees, she found a small cottage. Inside sat the monster, drinking tea and reading a book.

“You don’t look very frightening,” Mara said.

The monster sighed. “I try not to be.”

It wore ordinary clothes, baked bread on Sundays, and worried about the weather. It liked quiet music, tidy rooms, and strawberry jam. In nearly every way, it was normal.

“Then why does everyone call you a monster?” Mara asked.

“Because I look different,” it replied.

Mara returned to the village and told the people the truth. Most refused to believe her. They preferred the frightening story.

But Mara kept visiting the forest. And over time, she learned something important: sometimes the monster is normal, and sometimes fear is the truly monstrous thing.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, surrealist prose poem celebrating James Joyce’s *Ulysses*, filled with religious, sexual, linguistic, and Irish political imagery.
counterfactuals.output: Dublin wakes with a Latin tongue under its pillow, salt-white, sacramental, stammering: *Introibo*, says the sea, lifting its green chasuble over Sandymount, while every chimney exhales a small defeated republic. Leopold Bloom, wandering Jew of the butcher’s window and the perfumed envelope, carries the city in his pocket like a warm kidney wrapped in newsprint; Molly turns in the bed of Europe, dark rose, dark parliament, her thighs voting yes against the bishops, the barracks, the grave. Stephen’s skull is a cracked bell where Aristotle, Shakespeare, and the drowned mother quarrel in three languages, while the English crown squats on the postbox, red as a carbuncle, stamping empire upon love letters. O Eucharist of crumbs, soap, sweat, ink, and stout! O host raised in the tavern, where rhetoric fattens on porter and Parnell’s ghost slips a green carnation into the buttonhole of betrayal! The streets conjugate themselves—Dame Street, Eccles Street, Nighttown—each noun becoming flesh, each verb unbuttoned, each comma a little Liffey refusing the grammar of kings. In the brothel-mirror saints grow breasts, patriots grow asses’ ears, the citizen’s monocular thunder rolls its boulder toward Zion, and Bloom, mild heretic, answers hatred with a human hand. Printing presses copulate with catechisms; advertisements sprout angel wings; Gaelic, gagged in the schoolroom, returns as music, mockery, mouth-water, a rebel alphabet dancing naked on the Union Jack. All June dilates: one day becomes an odyssey, one city the world, one marriage bed a tribunal and temple. Then Molly, sovereign without crown, speaks from the warm republic of the body—memory, lust, Gibraltar, blood, flowers—until punctuation abdicates, dawn enters barefoot, and Ireland, that old sorrowful sow, dreams herself not conquered but endlessly uttered: yes the sea yes the word yes the wandering yes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an avant-garde modernist tribute to James Joyce in the style of Mina Loy, using fragmented syntax, extravagant metaphors, and almost no punctuation.
counterfactuals.output:
JOYCE  
with an alphabet of trapdoors  
under his tongue  

Dublin dilated  
a green pupil  
watching eternity misplace its hat  

he walked  
through the hour’s intestines  
collecting crumbs of god  
pub foam  
the obscene arithmetic of roses  

O cyclopean citizen  
O woman yesing the dark  
O sea with its blue grammar  
breaking syntax against the kidneys of stone  

his words  
mechanical peacocks  
dragging jeweled thunder  
through the domestic mud  

each comma exiled  
each noun undressed  
history a cracked mirror  
admiring its infinite bruises  

and language  
that old virgin machine  
suddenly pregnant  
with every nobody  

Bloom drifts  
a soft planet in trousers  
among advertisements  
funerals  
sandwiches  
the erotic furniture of noon  

while Stephen  
thin blade of metaphysics  
shaves the dawn  
from the dead face of Europe  

James  
you burglar of Babel  
you clockmaker stuffing stars  
into the pockets of one day  

still the city mutters you  
through rain  
through rancid gold  
through the mouth of the Liffey  

and night  
immense washerwoman  
wrings the last light  

yes  

into yes  

into the unpunctuated sea

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a Futurist poet reviewing *Ulysses* as a monstrous explosion of language, Catholicism, libido, Ireland, and rebellion against England.
counterfactuals.output:
### **JOYCE’S WORD-BOMB!**

At last—a book that does not walk but detonates!

*Ulysses* is a monstrous engine fueled by Guinness, Latin, lust, sea-salt, newspaper ink, Jesuit terror, Dublin mud, and the indigestible corpse of the British Empire. Joyce has crammed all Ireland into one day and fired it through the skull of Europe.

No plot! Plot is a policeman’s truncheon. Instead: acceleration, collision, catalogues, blasphemies, advertisements, chamber pots, Homeric ghosts! Language ceases to be the obedient valet of meaning and becomes a drunken dynamo, flinging puns, prayers, obscenities, scholastic riddles, and pub-talk against the cathedral walls.

Stephen Dedalus carries Catholicism like a cracked bell inside his brain. Every thought rings with guilt, incense, dead mothers, and rebellion. Bloom—magnificent urban animal!—wanders through Dublin with kidneys, cuckoldry, compassion, appetite, and advertisements revolving in his belly. Molly ends the book not with doctrine but with the body’s immense affirmative thunder: **YES!**

England hovers everywhere: ruler, censor, landlord, language. Yet Joyce sabotages English from within. He stuffs it with Irish rhythm, foreign debris, street cries, theological machinery, and erotic smoke until the imperial tongue swells, stammers, and bursts.

This is not a novel. It is a linguistic insurrection.

Burn the tidy sentence!  
Derail grammar!  
Electrify mythology!  
Turn the Mass into music-hall, history into hallucination, Dublin into the capital of the human nervous system!

*Ulysses* is obscene because life is obscene; Catholic because Ireland dreams in confessionals; rebellious because every word refuses to salute.

A book? No—

**A city-sized bomb, exploding forever in the mouth.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental stream-of-consciousness passage about Joyce as a “rejector-recreator,” blending Babel, Christ, Don Juan, Celtic culture, and the conflict between spirit and flesh.
counterfactuals.output:
Joyce, rejector-recreator, says no with a mouth full of yeses, breaks the tablets only to spell new commandments from the shards. Babel rises behind his eyes: brickword on brickword, tongues mortared with misunderstanding, Latin bells, Dublin curses, Hebrew thunder, French perfume, the wet consonants of the Celts. He rejects the tower and rebuilds it inward, a babelbody, every organ speaking its own exile.

And Christ passes through the sentence barefoot, wounded syntax, carrying the crossed beams of spirit and flesh. The spirit says Ascend. The flesh says Eat. The spirit says Renounce. The flesh, sly landlord of blood, says Another pint, another kiss, another warm mortal morning. Joyce hears both gospels and trusts neither entirely. For what resurrection can occur without a corpse? What word become flesh without first desiring the flesh it becomes?

Then Don Juan jingles at the chapel door, pockets bright with names, women, wagers, little absolutions. He is appetite wearing philosophy as a cloak. He kisses as though each mouth were the lost mother-language, each body a country briefly conquered and forever misunderstood. Christ looks at him; Don Juan winks. Between them Joyce places his pen, that thin black go-between, priest and pimp, spear and stem.

Ireland dreams under them, green not as innocence but as memory bruised into color. Tara murmurs through tenement walls. Cú Chulainn lifts his impossible arm in a public house mirror. The salmon of knowledge swims through sewerwater and Liffey foam, wise with refuse. Harps become rib cages; saints wear pagan shadows; the old gods, officially dead, keep breathing beneath the altarcloth. Celtic spirals curl into printer’s ink, turning and returning, never arriving except where they began—which is not the same place, no, never the same.

Reject, recreate. Reject the fatherland, remake it syllable by syllable. Reject the Church, retain its incense in the lungs. Reject purity, baptize the obscene. Reject the English tongue, then seize it, stretch it, make it stammer Irishly, make the conqueror’s language carry the conquered dream. Babel is not punishment now but possibility: all tongues fallen together, promiscuous, comic, divine.

Yet the quarrel persists. Soul against skin. Halo against hunger. The pale host lifted above the red feast of the body. Spirit wants eternity because it fears touch; flesh wants touch because it knows eternity is cold. Joyce walks between them, spectacles flashing, laughing perhaps, or coughing, his eyes full of nightprint. He will not reconcile them. Reconciliation is too clean. He knots them instead: Christ’s wound with Don Juan’s kiss, Celtic mist with city soot, prayer with pun, martyrdom with digestion.

And from the knot comes the bookbeast, many-tongued, half angel half animal, crawling toward dawn while remembering midnight. It says: I deny, therefore I make. I flee, therefore I carry home inside me. I sin in order to know what salvation has excluded. I praise the flesh until it becomes spirit; I drag spirit down until it sweats.

The tower falls.

The tower begins.

In the rubble, every broken word opens an eye.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
